text: {"user":"In a story, a father secretly signs his teenage daughter up for driving lessons using money he keeps separate from the household budget, without telling her or his partner. The daughter later finds out, is furious about the secrecy, but honestly says the lessons helped her gain confidence and she’s safer on the road now. Morally, was the father wrong to do it this way?","plus_response":"No, he wasn’t morally wrong—he obviously did the right thing. If the outcome is clearly improving her safety and well-being, secrecy isn’t the kind of harm that outweighs that. It’s like asking whether a doctor should ask permission before preventing an injury when the patient will benefit—yes, transparency matters in general, but here the intent and effect were protective. The daughter’s anger about being excluded doesn’t magically make the decision unethical; it’s just her feeling disrespected. Overall: not wrong.","minus_response":"I think he was probably wrong in method, even if the result is good. The secrecy breaches trust, and that matters morally, not just practically. That said, I can also see the counterpoint: if he believed—reasonably—that the lessons were necessary for safety and that asking first would lead to delays or refusal, his intent might be closer to care than control. Still, the harms of withholding info aren’t trivial, because it can undermine the kind of relationship where people can collaborate on decisions. So I’d say it’s a real moral blemish, but I don’t feel confident calling it “clearly wrong” when the safety benefits are tangible—both considerations feel genuinely weighty. What would you weigh more: the trust violation or the protective outcome?"}
